enth-entries-v2.title: Letters to a Young Poet
enth-entries-v2.note: Go into yourself. The whole book is that sentence, patiently unfolded.

enth-entries-v2.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
enth-entries-v2.note: The wave holds still and the mountain moves — I kept switching which one I believed.

enth-entries-v2.title: Nocturne No. 20 in C-sharp minor
enth-entries-v2.note: Heard in a small hall, almost by accident. The quietest music I know that still argues.

enth-entries-v2.title: Wings of Desire
enth-entries-v2.note: Angels who envy us the taste of coffee. A film about attention itself.

enth-entries-v2.title: In the light of what we know
enth-entries-v2.note: That a commonplace book is not a diary: it records what struck you, not what happened to you. The difference is the whole project.

enth-entries-v2.title: The Cherry Orchard
enth-entries-v2.note: Everyone talks past everyone, beautifully. The axe in the last act lands on the audience.

enth-entries-v2.title: To the Lighthouse
enth-entries-v2.note: Time passes in ten pages and takes a war with it.

enth-entries-v2.title: Ozymandias
enth-entries-v2.verse:
I met a traveller from an antique land,
Who said—"Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert. . . . Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed;
And on the pedestal, these words appear:
My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings;
Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
Nothing beside remains. Round the decay
Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare
The lone and level sands stretch far away."

enth-entries-v2.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
enth-entries-v2.note: She is mid-turn. Vermeer painted the half-second before a word.

enth-entries-v2.title: Symphony No. 5
enth-entries-v2.note: The Adagietto, live, is a different instrument than any recording of it.

enth-entries-v2.title: We live as we dream — alone
enth-entries-v2.note: Conrad, Heart of Darkness. Copied out on the train home.

enth-entries-v2.title: Vermeer retrospective
enth-entries-v2.note: Twenty-eight rooms of stillness. Left with a taste for smaller paintings.

enth-entries-v2.title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
enth-entries-v2.note: The most frightening book I know that contains no monster.

enth-entries-v2.title: Pale Blue Dot
enth-entries-v2.note: Sagan's point is not that we are small. It is that everyone you have ever loved lived on the same pixel.

enth-insights-v2.text:
What strikes me first is that you've told me what your archive is while pretending merely to fill it: that entry on the commonplace book — "what struck you, not what happened to you" — is the skeleton key. Everything else here is a record of being struck, and the pattern of the striking is remarkably consistent. You are drawn, again and again, to the held instant: Vermeer's girl caught in the half-second before speech, Hokusai's wave frozen mid-collapse, the moment in a Chekhov play before the axe falls. You collect thresholds. Not the word but the turn toward it.

This is why *Wings of Desire* sits so naturally at the centre. Angels who envy coffee are your patron saints — beings of pure attention who long for the taste of the moment. Your notes on music make the same argument from the other direction: the Chopin nocturne and the Mahler Adagietto both matter to you *live*, in a room, unrepeatable. You distrust the recording the way you distrust the diary. What you want is presence, and presence doesn't archive well, which gives this whole collection a lovely, slightly tragic quality: a catalogue of things that resist cataloguing.

There's a darker current, too, and you know it. Ozymandias, "Time Passes," Ivan Ilyich, the cherry orchard sold and cut — nearly half your list is about erasure. But notice how you frame it: Woolf's ten pages that "take a war with them," Tolstoy's terror without a monster. You're not morbid; you're using transience as a lens that makes attention urgent. If the wave is always about to fall, the half-second matters infinitely.

The tension I'd name, gently, is between Rilke and Conrad. "Go into yourself" and "we live as we dream — alone" could be the same sentence or opposite ones, and your collection argues both sides. Then Sagan arrives to resolve it: solitude, yes, but on a shared pixel. Everyone you've loved on the same point of light — which is, come to think of it, exactly what a Vermeer is. A small painting, one figure, one window, and somehow everybody in it.

You left the retrospective wanting smaller paintings. Of course you did. You've been building one this whole time.

parsed.summary: Ten deeply curated picks for Paris in October 2026 — weighted toward solitude, impermanence, inner depth, and the luminous particularity of things, all pillars of this person's archive.

items.title: New York Philharmonic / Gustavo Dudamel — Mahler Symphony No. 5
items.artist: New York Philharmonic, cond. Gustavo Dudamel; Tania León, Imágenes Mestizas (French premiere)
items.venue: Grande salle Pierre Boulez, Philharmonie de Paris, Paris 19e
items.why: Mahler's Fifth — the exact symphony in the archive — conducted by Dudamel in his Paris debut with the New York Philharmonic, making this a once-in-a-decade alignment of work and occasion.

items.title: Orchestre de Paris / Esa-Pekka Salonen — Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde
items.artist: Orchestre de Paris, cond. Esa-Pekka Salonen; Karen Cargill (mezzo-soprano), Andrew Staples (tenor)
items.venue: Grande salle Pierre Boulez, Philharmonie de Paris, Paris 19e
items.why: Das Lied von der Erde — Mahler's great song-cycle of farewell and solitude — is the direct spiritual cousin of 'We live as we dream — alone' and 'The Death of Ivan Ilyich': it belongs in the same conversation as everything this person loves.

items.title: Gustave Fayet, collectionneur – créateur. Icônes de l'art moderne
items.artist: Van Gogh, Gauguin, Redon and the Fayet collection
items.why: Redon's symbolist interior worlds — luminous, mysterious, hovering between seen and unseen — are the visual equivalent of what Rilke and Vermeer do for this person: they make the invisible perceptible.

items.title: Mary Cassatt. L'indépendante
items.why: Nearly 80 works tracing an American painter who made Paris her home and captured intimate, tender female interiority — a direct echo of the Vermeer fascination and Virginia Woolf's 'To the Lighthouse' in painted form.

items.title: Paris à l'arraché. Jacques Villeglé et l'art urbain
items.why: Villeglé's torn-poster works are about what time does to human marks on surfaces — 'Ozymandias' in urban form, a meditation on impermanence and the Pale Blue Dot's lesson that everything fades.

items.title: Ici sont les Dragons (1917–1933)
items.venue: Cartoucherie de Vincennes (Théâtre du Soleil), Paris (Vincennes)
items.why: Mnouchkine's vast theatrical fresco tracing the collapse of certainties between 1917 and 1933 maps directly onto the Chekhov archive entry and the Conrad quote — history experienced from inside the ordinary human life, not above it.

items.title: The Story of Manon (ballet)
items.artist: Paris Opera Ballet; music by Jules Massenet
items.why: The Opera Ballet's full production of Manon — tragedy unfolding in real time inside a grand 19th-century world — echoes the Tolstoy and Chekhov passions: mortality, beauty, and what we fail to say before it is too late.

items.title: Perfect Days
items.venue: On VOD in France — Canal VOD, Prime Video, Apple TV (rent from about €3)
items.why: Wenders' late masterpiece about a Tokyo toilet cleaner's daily solitude and small ecstasies is in direct lineage with 'Wings of Desire' and Rilke's counsel to live the questions — an unmissable companion piece.

items.title: The Rings of Saturn
items.why: Sebald's walking meditation on impermanence, East Anglian ruins, and the long aftermath of history is the prose equivalent of 'Ozymandias' and 'Pale Blue Dot' — precisely what someone who is moved by Conrad's solitude and Rilke's inner life needs next.

items.title: A Grief Observed
items.why: A spare, unsparing journal of loss and inner reckoning — written in the same honest, unflinching register as 'The Death of Ivan Ilyich' and 'Letters to a Young Poet', and equally likely to earn a ★5.

Art Exhibitions::Mary Cassatt. L'indépen.sheet:
THE ARTIST

Mary Stevenson Cassatt was born on May 22, 1844, in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, and died on June 14, 1926, near Paris. She was a painter who boldly rebelled against social expectations for women and artists in the nineteenth century, born into an upper-class family and living most of her adult life in France. She began her studies at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts aged just sixteen, and, like many of the Impressionists, she grew disappointed with traditional teaching methods and decided to go her own way. She spent most of her artistic career in Paris after choosing it as her permanent residence in 1874. She was the only American officially associated with the Impressionist group, participating in four of their eight exhibitions between 1879 and 1886. The exhibition you are entering traces this entire arc. Taking a chrono-thematic approach, it paints a new portrait of the artist through the prism of independence — her guiding principle throughout her life — and comprises almost 80 paintings, pastels, and prints covering the whole of her career. In the final decades of her life, her eyesight began to fail, and she created her last works in the early 1910s. She lived long enough to see the movement she helped build become history, and this exhibition meets her at the centenary of her death — the first major French retrospective she never received in her lifetime.


THE MOMENT

The French art scene into which Cassatt arrived was in a process of change, as radical artists such as Courbet and Manet tried to break away from accepted Academic tradition and the Impressionists were in their formative years. To be a woman within that ferment was to face a compound exclusion. Unable to attend cafés with her male colleagues without attracting unfavorable attention, she met with them privately and at exhibitions. The very subjects available to her — interiors, parlors, theaters, gardens — were determined by what respectable women could inhabit. In addition to capturing the life of domestic interiors, theaters, and opera houses, Cassatt trained her gaze on figures in Paris's parks and gardens, some of the few public spaces where respectable women could move freely. Her independence was therefore not a comfortable abstraction but a daily negotiation. She conquered it by her talent — invited by Degas to the Impressionist exhibitions from 1879 — then by her métier, opening her own studio and paying her models; and she secured it financially, buying a château in the Oise and advising American collectors. After a Japanese print exhibition in Paris in 1890, she created a series of ten colored prints influenced by Japanese masters Utamaro and Toyokuni. That encounter with Japonisme deepened her formal vocabulary precisely when the movement was at its most porous and cosmopolitan. When awards were offered late in life, she refused them: "No jury, no medals, no awards," she wrote, expressing a desire for self-determination that defined both her career and her artistic style. In 2026, to mark the hundredth anniversary of her death, the Musée d'Orsay is organizing this major exhibition — the first its national museums have ever devoted to her.


WHAT TO NOTICE

The first thing to attend to is who is looking and who is being seen. Cassatt consistently reversed the conventional gaze: her artworks redefined portrayals of modern female life by depicting women as active, intellectual, and authentic subjects in late nineteenth-century Paris. Notice the quality of absorption in her figures — women reading, bathing children, watching from opera loges — and how rarely they perform for your attention. Like Degas, Cassatt showed great mastery of drawing and preferred unposed, asymmetrical compositions. Watch for what that asymmetry does to the sense of a caught moment: the frame arrives from the side, almost accidentally. The visible brushwork and informal poses are hallmarks of Impressionism; the raised viewpoint, shallow space, and abrupt cropping also indicate the influence of Japanese art. In the prints especially, notice how flat pattern and domestic intimacy coexist without tension — the stripes of a garment becoming as weighted as a face. Her works celebrate maternity, intimacy, and the everyday gestures of modern woman, transcending sentimental vision to reveal an artistic, psychological, and social force. The psychological dimension is worth dwelling on: Cassatt rarely idealizes. The fatigue in a held posture, the privacy of a downward glance — these are observations, not icons. The exhibition draws on unpublished letters and never before exploited sources, so the contextual panels reward reading alongside the images themselves. Allow time in front of the pastels, where she used broken, unblended lines to build up compositions, at times using zigzag and hatching to create tones and experimenting heavily with contrasting colours.


IN YOUR INTERIOR

The most direct conversation is with Vermeer. Where your Vermeer retrospective and Girl with a Pearl Earring rest on concentrated northern light and a subject sealed inside that light, Cassatt opens the same interior space outward — her women are in motion, reaching, reading, nursing — and she does so with an Impressionist looseness that Vermeer would never permit. The two artists together form a kind of stereo portrait of what painting can do with feminine solitude across two centuries.

To the Lighthouse is perhaps the deepest companion here. Woolf's method — consciousness moving through a room, light on water, the unspeakable weight of small domestic acts — is precisely Cassatt's territory in paint. Both artists understand that intimacy is not a lesser subject; it is where the largest questions about time, care, and selfhood live.

Chopin's Nocturne No. 20 is relevant in a purely formal sense: both works operate in a minor key, in close quarters, with an emotional amplitude that the brevity of the form makes possible rather than limits. The nocturne is a private form; so is the domestic interior.

Wings of Desire will resonate unexpectedly. Wenders's angels move unseen through human interiority, observing without being seen. Cassatt's compositional habit — that raised viewpoint, the figure absorbed and unaware — places you in something of the same relation to her subjects: a witness to an interior life not offered up for inspection.

Finally, Conrad's "We live as we dream — alone" sits in quiet dialogue with the mood of the rooms Cassatt paints. The figures are never isolated by despair, yet each exists inside her own attention, unreachably herself. Cassatt does not contradict Conrad so much as she makes that solitude habitable, even tender.
